lessons.title: Cell Structure and Microscopy
lessons.description: Eukaryotic vs prokaryotic cells, organelle functions and the power of microscopes.
lessons.content_html:
Eukaryotic and Prokaryotic Cells

All living organisms are made of cells. There are two fundamental types of cell: eukaryotic cells and prokaryotic cells. Eukaryotic cells are found in animals and plants. They are complex, with a nucleus that holds the cell's genetic material. Prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, are much smaller and simpler, with no true nucleus.

Animal cells contain the following sub-cellular structures:

  • Nucleus — contains genetic material (DNA) that controls the cell's activities.
  • Cell membrane — controls what enters and leaves the cell; it is selectively permeable.
  • Mitochondria — the site of aerobic respiration, where energy is transferred from glucose.
  • Ribosomes — tiny structures where proteins are synthesised (made).

Plant cells have all of these structures plus some additional ones:

  • Cell wall — a rigid outer layer made of cellulose that provides support and protection.
  • Chloroplasts — contain chlorophyll, the green pigment that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
  • Vacuole — a large, permanent structure filled with cell sap that helps maintain the cell's shape.

Key Fact

Bacterial (prokaryotic) cells have chromosomal DNA that floats freely in the cytoplasm (no nucleus), plasmid DNA (small rings of extra DNA), a cell membrane, ribosomes, and some have a flagellum for movement. They do NOT have mitochondria or chloroplasts.

Specialised Cells

Cells become specialised to carry out particular functions. This process is called differentiation. The Edexcel specification requires you to know three examples of specialised cells.

Sperm cells are adapted for fertilisation:

  • An acrosome at the tip releases enzymes to penetrate the egg cell.
  • A haploid nucleus carries half the genetic information so a full set is restored at fertilisation.
  • Many mitochondria in the middle section provide energy for the tail to swim.
  • A long tail (flagellum) enables the sperm to move towards the egg.

Egg cells (ova) are adapted for fertilisation and early development:

  • They contain nutrients in the cytoplasm to nourish the early embryo after fertilisation.
  • They have a haploid nucleus, so the full diploid number is restored when the sperm fuses with the egg.
  • After fertilisation, the cell membrane changes structure to prevent more than one sperm from entering. This is essential to maintain the correct chromosome number.

Ciliated epithelial cells line the airways (trachea and bronchi). They have tiny hair-like projections called cilia on their surface that beat rhythmically. This sweeps mucus (which has trapped dust and microorganisms) upwards towards the throat, keeping the lungs clean.

Key Fact

Cells become specialised through differentiation, so their structure is adapted to suit their function: sperm cells have a tail and many mitochondria for swimming, egg cells store nutrients for the embryo, and ciliated epithelial cells use cilia to sweep mucus out of the airways.

Microscopy

Cells are far too small to see with the naked eye, so scientists use microscopes to study them. A light microscope uses light and glass lenses. Light microscopes are cheap, portable and can show living cells in colour, but they only magnify up to about ×2000 and cannot show small sub-cellular structures clearly.

An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light. This gives a much higher magnification (over ×1,000,000) and a much higher resolution, so scientists can see tiny sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and the internal detail of mitochondria. However, electron microscopes are large, very expensive, and the specimen must be dead.

Resolution is the ability to tell apart two points that are very close together. Because electron microscopes have a much higher resolution than light microscopes, they reveal far more detail — this is what allowed scientists to discover sub-cellular structures.

Magnification tells you how many times larger an image is than the real object. It is calculated using the formula:

\(\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{real size}}\)

You can rearrange this to find the real size or the image size. Always make sure both measurements are in the same units before calculating — for example, convert millimetres (mm) to micrometres (µm) by multiplying by 1000.

For example, if a cell is 50 µm wide in real life and appears 100 mm wide in a photograph, first convert 100 mm to 100,000 µm, then magnification = 100,000 ÷ 50 = ×2000.

Key Fact

Magnification = image size ÷ real size. Electron microscopes have much higher magnification and resolution than light microscopes, so they can show sub-cellular structures. Always convert both measurements to the same units before you calculate.

lessons.title: Enzymes and Transport
lessons.description: How enzymes work, factors affecting activity, and transport across cell membranes.
lessons.content_html:
Enzymes and the Active Site

Enzymes are biological catalysts. They speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being used up or changed permanently. Without enzymes, the reactions needed for life would happen far too slowly.

Each enzyme has a specific shape, including a region called the active site. The substrate (the molecule the enzyme acts on) fits into the active site like a key fitting into a lock. This is called the lock and key model. The enzyme is specific to its substrate — only a substrate with the correct complementary shape can bind to the active site.

Once the substrate binds, the enzyme lowers the activation energy needed for the reaction. The products are released, and the enzyme is free to catalyse another reaction.

Key Fact

Enzyme specificity means each enzyme only catalyses one type of reaction. The shape of the active site is complementary to only one substrate. If the shape changes (e.g. by high temperature or extreme pH), the substrate can no longer fit.

Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity

Temperature: As temperature increases, enzyme activity increases because molecules move faster and collide more frequently with the active site. However, above the optimum temperature (typically around 37°C for human enzymes), the enzyme begins to denature. The bonds holding the active site in shape break, the shape changes permanently, and the substrate can no longer fit.

pH: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it works fastest. Moving away from this optimum in either direction reduces enzyme activity. Extreme pH values cause the active site to change shape (denaturing the enzyme). For example, pepsin in the stomach works best at pH 2, while amylase in the mouth works best at around pH 7.

Substrate concentration: Increasing substrate concentration increases the rate of reaction because there are more substrate molecules to collide with the active sites. However, at very high concentrations, the rate levels off because all active sites are occupied — the enzyme is said to be saturated.

Core Practical: Investigating the Effect of pH on Enzyme Activity

In this core practical, you investigate how pH affects the rate at which amylase breaks down starch. You set up test tubes with amylase and starch at different pH values using buffer solutions. At regular intervals, you take a sample and test it with iodine solution. Iodine turns blue-black in the presence of starch. You record the time for the iodine to stop changing colour (meaning all starch has been digested). The shorter the time, the faster the enzyme activity.

Rate of reaction = 1 ÷ time. You can plot rate against pH to find the optimum pH for amylase.

Enzymes in Digestion

Enzymes play a vital role in digestion. Large, insoluble food molecules must be broken down into smaller, soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the blood.

  • Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates into simple sugars (e.g. amylase breaks starch into maltose and then glucose).
  • Proteases break down proteins into amino acids.
  • Lipases break down lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol.

Enzymes are also essential for synthesis — building large molecules from smaller ones. For example, enzymes join amino acids together to form proteins, and join simple sugars together to form complex carbohydrates like starch and glycogen.

Key Fact

In the exam, you need to know that enzymes catalyse both the breakdown AND the synthesis of biological molecules: carbohydrates ↔ sugars, proteins ↔ amino acids, lipids ↔ fatty acids + glycerol.

Transport Across Cell Membranes

Substances must move into and out of cells for the cell to function. There are three key transport mechanisms you need to know.

Diffusion is the net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. It is a passive process — no energy is required. It occurs because particles are constantly moving randomly. Examples include oxygen diffusing into cells for respiration and carbon dioxide diffusing out as a waste product.

Osmosis is a special case of diffusion. It is the movement of water molecules from a dilute solution (high water concentration) to a more concentrated solution (low water concentration) through a partially permeable membrane. The cell membrane is partially permeable.

Active transport moves substances from a lower concentration to a higher concentration — against the concentration gradient. This requires energy from cellular respiration. An example is the absorption of mineral ions by plant root hair cells from the soil, where the mineral concentration is lower in the soil than inside the root cell.

Core Practical: Investigating Osmosis in Potatoes

In this core practical, you cut potato cylinders of equal length and mass, then place them in sucrose solutions of different concentrations. After a set time (e.g. 30 minutes), you remove them, blot dry, and re-measure their mass. In dilute solutions, the potato gains mass (water moves in by osmosis). In concentrated solutions, the potato loses mass (water moves out). You calculate percentage change in mass using: (final mass − initial mass) ÷ initial mass × 100.

Key Fact

Diffusion and osmosis are passive (no energy needed). Active transport requires energy from respiration and moves substances against the concentration gradient. Know the direction of movement for each process.

lessons.title: Cell Division and Stem Cells
lessons.description: Mitosis, the cell cycle, cancer, growth and the promise of stem cell research.
lessons.content_html:
The Cell Cycle and Mitosis

Cells divide to produce new cells for growth, repair and replacement. The process of cell division in body cells is called mitosis. Mitosis is part of the cell cycle — the repeating sequence of growth and division that cells go through.

The cell cycle has several stages. Before mitosis begins, the cell goes through interphase, during which the cell grows, carries out its normal functions, and makes a copy of every chromosome (DNA replication). Once interphase is complete, mitosis can begin.

The Edexcel specification requires you to know the stages of mitosis:

  • Prophase — chromosomes condense and become visible. The nuclear membrane starts to break down.
  • Metaphase — chromosomes line up along the middle (equator) of the cell.
  • Anaphase — the two copies of each chromosome are pulled apart to opposite ends (poles) of the cell by spindle fibres.
  • Telophase — a new nuclear membrane forms around each set of chromosomes. The chromosomes begin to uncoil.
  • Cytokinesis — the cytoplasm divides, producing two separate daughter cells.

Key Fact

Mitosis produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to each other AND to the parent cell. Each daughter cell is diploid — it has the full set of chromosomes. Remember the order: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase (PMAT).

Importance of Mitosis

Mitosis is important for three key reasons:

  • Growth — organisms grow by producing more cells through mitosis.
  • Repair — damaged or worn-out cells are replaced by identical new cells made through mitosis (e.g. skin cells replacing a wound).
  • Asexual reproduction — some organisms reproduce by mitosis alone, producing offspring that are genetically identical to the parent (clones). For example, strawberry plants send out runners, and bacteria divide by binary fission.

Cancer

Cancer occurs when changes (mutations) in a cell's DNA cause the cell to divide uncontrollably. Normal cells have checkpoints in the cell cycle that prevent division when it is not needed. In cancer, these controls fail. The rapidly dividing cells form a mass called a tumour. Some tumours are benign (stay in one place), but malignant tumours can spread to other parts of the body.

Growth in Organisms

Growth happens differently in animals and plants:

  • Animals grow by cell division (mitosis) and then cell differentiation — cells become specialised for particular functions.
  • Plants grow by cell division, cell elongation (cells stretch and lengthen), and cell differentiation.

Percentile charts are used to monitor growth in children. They show how a child's height or weight compares to others of the same age. For example, if a child is on the 75th percentile for height, it means 75% of children of the same age are shorter. Doctors use percentile charts to check for potential growth problems — a child who drops significantly across percentile lines might need further investigation.

Key Fact

Plant growth differs from animal growth because it involves cell elongation as well as cell division and differentiation. Most plant growth occurs at the tips of roots and shoots, where meristems are located.

Stem Cells

Stem cells are undifferentiated cells — they have not yet become specialised. They can divide to produce more stem cells or differentiate into different types of specialised cell.

There are different types of stem cell:

  • Embryonic stem cells — found in early embryos. These can differentiate into almost any type of cell in the body. They have the greatest potential for medical use.
  • Adult stem cells — found in some adult tissues (e.g. bone marrow). These can only differentiate into a limited range of cell types. For example, bone marrow stem cells can produce different types of blood cell.
  • Meristems — found in plants at the tips of roots and shoots. Meristem cells can differentiate into any type of plant cell throughout the plant's life. This is why plants continue growing for their entire lifespan.
Stem Cells in Medicine: Benefits and Risks

Stem cells offer exciting possibilities in medicine. They could be used to replace damaged or diseased cells — for example, replacing faulty insulin-producing cells in type 1 diabetes, or repairing damaged nerve cells after spinal injuries.

However, there are also risks and ethical concerns. The use of embryonic stem cells is controversial because it involves the destruction of embryos. There are also medical risks — stem cells could divide uncontrollably and cause tumours. The body's immune system may reject transplanted stem cells. Adult stem cell treatments are less controversial but are more limited in what they can differentiate into.

Key Fact

In the exam, you may be asked to discuss the benefits and risks of stem cell use. Benefits: potential to treat diseases like diabetes, Parkinson's, and paralysis. Risks: tumour formation, immune rejection, ethical issues around embryo destruction. Balance both sides in your answer.

lessons.title: The Nervous System
lessons.description: Neurones, synapses, reflex arcs and how the nervous system coordinates responses.
lessons.content_html:
The Nervous System: An Overview

The nervous system allows organisms to detect changes in their environment and respond to them. It enables rapid communication between different parts of the body. The human nervous system consists of the central nervous system (CNS) — the brain and spinal cord — and the peripheral nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.

The nervous system works through a sequence of events: a stimulus is detected by a receptor, an electrical impulse travels along neurones to the CNS, the CNS processes the information, and a response is carried out by an effector (a muscle or gland).

Key Fact

The pathway is: Stimulus → Receptor → Sensory neurone → CNS (relay neurone) → Motor neurone → Effector → Response. Receptors detect changes; effectors carry out responses.

Types of Neurone

There are three types of neurone (nerve cell) that you need to know:

Sensory neurones carry electrical impulses from receptors to the CNS. Receptors are specialised cells that detect stimuli — for example, light receptors in the eye detect light, and temperature receptors in the skin detect heat changes.

Relay neurones are found in the CNS (brain and spinal cord). They connect sensory neurones to motor neurones and process the information.

Motor neurones carry electrical impulses from the CNS to effectors (muscles or glands). When a muscle receives an impulse, it contracts. When a gland receives an impulse, it secretes a chemical such as a hormone.

Neurone Structure

Neurones have specialised structures that enable them to transmit electrical impulses efficiently:

  • Cell body — contains the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm and organelles.
  • Dendron — a long fibre that carries impulses towards the cell body. It branches into dendrites at the end, which connect to other neurones or receptors.
  • Axon — a long fibre that carries impulses away from the cell body towards the next neurone or effector. The axon can be very long (e.g. from the spinal cord to the toes).
  • Myelin sheath — a fatty, insulating layer that surrounds the axon. The myelin sheath speeds up the transmission of electrical impulses by insulating the axon and causing the impulse to jump between gaps in the sheath.

Key Fact

Dendron carries impulses TOWARDS the cell body. Axon carries impulses AWAY from the cell body. The myelin sheath speeds up impulse transmission. Remember these directions — they are commonly tested.

Synapses

Neurones do not physically touch each other. There is a tiny gap between them called a synapse. Electrical impulses cannot jump across this gap. Instead, the signal is transmitted chemically:

  1. An electrical impulse arrives at the end of the first neurone (the pre-synaptic neurone).
  2. This triggers the release of chemical neurotransmitters from vesicles into the synaptic gap.
  3. The neurotransmitters diffuse across the gap.
  4. They bind to specific receptors on the membrane of the second neurone (the post-synaptic neurone).
  5. This triggers a new electrical impulse in the second neurone.

Synapses ensure that impulses travel in one direction only — from the pre-synaptic neurone to the post-synaptic neurone. This is because neurotransmitters are only released from one side and receptors are only on the other side.

The Reflex Arc

A reflex action is a rapid, automatic response to a potentially dangerous stimulus. Reflexes are faster than voluntary responses because they do not involve conscious thought — the impulse is processed by the spinal cord rather than the brain.

The pathway for a reflex action is called a reflex arc:

  1. Stimulus — e.g. touching a hot object.
  2. Receptor — pain receptors in the skin detect the stimulus.
  3. Sensory neurone — carries the impulse to the spinal cord.
  4. Relay neurone — in the spinal cord, passes the impulse directly to a motor neurone (no brain involvement).
  5. Motor neurone — carries the impulse to the effector.
  6. Effector — a muscle contracts to pull the hand away from the hot object.

Key Fact

In a reflex arc, the relay neurone is in the spinal cord (not the brain). This is what makes reflexes fast — the signal takes the shortest possible route. Reflexes protect the body from damage before you are even aware of the danger.

Examples of Reflex Actions

Common examples include: pulling your hand away from a hot surface (pain reflex), the pupil constricting in bright light (pupil reflex), and blinking when something approaches your eye. In each case, the response is automatic and rapid, protecting the body from potential harm.

You can investigate human responses to stimuli in a practical — for example, the ruler drop test measures reaction time. This is a voluntary response, so it is slower than a true reflex. Factors such as caffeine, tiredness, or distractions can affect reaction times.

Key Fact

At a synapse, the signal changes from electrical to chemical (neurotransmitter) and back to electrical. Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synaptic gap and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new impulse.

lessons.title: Genetics and DNA
lessons.description: DNA structure, meiosis, monohybrid inheritance and the Human Genome Project.
lessons.content_html:
The Structure of DNA

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer made of two strands coiled together to form a double helix. The two strands are linked by pairs of complementary bases joined by weak hydrogen bonds.

Each strand is built from repeating units called nucleotides. Every nucleotide has three parts: a sugar, a phosphate group and one of four bases — adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) or guanine (G). The bases always pair in a fixed pattern: A with T and C with G. This is called complementary base pairing.

Key Fact

DNA is a double helix of nucleotides. Each nucleotide = sugar + phosphate + base. Bases pair A–T and C–G, joined by weak hydrogen bonds.

Genomes and Genes

The genome is the entire DNA of an organism. A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a specific protein. The order of bases along a gene acts as a code, telling the cell which amino acids to join together to make that protein. Different proteins give an organism its characteristics.

There is usually extensive genetic variation within a population of a species. This variation arises through mutations. Most genetic mutations have no effect on the phenotype. Some have a small effect, and only rarely does a single mutation significantly change the phenotype.

Meiosis

Meiosis is the type of cell division that produces gametes — sex cells. Unlike mitosis, meiosis produces four genetically different haploid daughter cells, each with half the chromosome number of the parent cell. The stages of meiosis are not required for this specification.

In humans, body cells are diploid with 46 chromosomes. Meiosis halves this to 23 per gamete. At fertilisation, two gametes fuse and the full diploid number (46) is restored in the zygote.

Key Fact

Meiosis produces 4 genetically different haploid gametes. Fertilisation restores the diploid number. This is why offspring from sexual reproduction show genetic variation.

You can extract DNA from strawberries by mashing the fruit, adding salt water and washing-up liquid to break open cells, filtering the mixture, then carefully layering ice-cold ethanol on top. DNA precipitates as white, stringy threads at the boundary between the two liquids.

Alleles and Inheritance

An allele is a version of a gene. Organisms inherit two alleles for each gene — one from each parent. If both alleles are the same the organism is homozygous; if different it is heterozygous. A dominant allele is expressed whenever it is present. A recessive allele is only expressed in the homozygous state.

The combination of alleles is the genotype. The observable characteristic it produces is the phenotype. Most phenotypic features result from multiple genes, not single-gene inheritance.

Monohybrid Crosses and Punnett Squares

A monohybrid cross tracks one gene with two alleles. A Punnett square shows all possible offspring genotypes. For example, crossing two heterozygous parents (Bb × Bb) gives genotypes BB, Bb, Bb and bb — a 3:1 phenotype ratio (3 dominant : 1 recessive).

You must be able to calculate probabilities, ratios and percentages from these crosses. In the example above there is a 75% (\(\frac{3}{4}\)) chance of the dominant phenotype and a 25% (\(\frac{1}{4}\)) chance of the recessive phenotype. Family pedigree diagrams can also be used to trace the inheritance of alleles across generations.

Key Fact

Use Punnett squares to predict offspring genotypes and phenotypes. Bb × Bb gives 3:1 dominant : recessive. Calculate outcomes as ratios, fractions or percentages.

Sex Determination

The 23rd pair of chromosomes determines biological sex. Females have two X chromosomes (XX); males have one X and one Y (XY). Each egg carries an X chromosome. Sperm carry either X or Y. If an X-carrying sperm fertilises the egg the offspring is female; if a Y-carrying sperm fertilises the egg the offspring is male. This gives a 50:50 chance, which you can show with a Punnett square.

Variation

Variation in phenotype has two causes. Genetic variation arises from mutations and from sexual reproduction (meiosis shuffles alleles, and fertilisation creates new combinations). Environmental variation comes from an organism’s surroundings — for example, diet, climate or exercise. Most phenotypic features are influenced by both.

The Human Genome Project mapped every gene in human DNA. Potential applications include identifying genes linked to diseases, developing personalised medicines, improving understanding of human evolution and migration, and creating genetic tests to assess the risk of inherited conditions.

lessons.title: Evolution and Classification
lessons.description: Darwin's theory, fossil evidence for human evolution and the classification of organisms.
lessons.content_html:
Darwin’s Theory of Evolution by Natural Selection

Charles Darwin proposed the theory of natural selection. His theory can be summarised in four steps:

First, within any population there is variation — individuals have different characteristics due to differences in their alleles. Second, organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support, leading to a struggle for survival. Third, individuals with characteristics best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce. Fourth, these advantageous alleles are passed on to the next generation, so over time the population changes.

Key Fact

Natural selection: variation in a population → struggle for survival → best-adapted individuals survive and reproduce → advantageous alleles passed to offspring → population changes over time.

Antibiotic Resistance as Evidence for Evolution

The emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria supports Darwin’s theory. Within a bacterial population, random mutations may produce an individual that is resistant to an antibiotic. When the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed, but the resistant bacterium survives. It reproduces rapidly, passing the resistance allele to its offspring. Over time, the population becomes dominated by resistant bacteria. This is natural selection in action.

MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is an example of a bacterium that has evolved resistance to several antibiotics. This is why doctors are encouraged to prescribe antibiotics only when necessary and patients must complete the full course.

Evidence for Human Evolution — Fossils

Fossils provide evidence for human evolution. The Edexcel specification requires you to know three key fossil discoveries:

Ardi (Ardipithecus ramidus) dates from about 4.4 million years ago. Ardi had both ape-like features (long arms, an opposable big toe for gripping branches) and human-like features (she could walk upright on two legs, at least some of the time). This suggests she was an early stage in the evolution from apes to humans.

Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) dates from about 3.2 million years ago. Lucy had a smaller brain than modern humans but her skeleton shows she walked upright more efficiently than Ardi. Her knee and hip joints were adapted for bipedal walking, showing that walking upright evolved before large brains.

Richard Leakey’s discovery from about 1.6 million years ago (often called Turkana Boy) was a nearly complete skeleton of Homo erectus. This individual was tall, had a relatively large brain, and had a body shape much more like modern humans. These three fossils show a gradual change over millions of years from ape-like ancestors to modern humans.

Key Fact

Three key fossils: Ardi (4.4 million years ago), Lucy (3.2 mya) and Leakey’s Homo erectus (1.6 mya). They show a gradual progression from ape-like to human-like features.

Evidence from Stone Tools

Stone tools also provide evidence for human evolution. The earliest tools were simple pebble tools, used for cutting and scraping. Over time, tools became more sophisticated — hand axes, blades and eventually finely crafted arrowheads. This development shows increasing brain capacity and problem-solving ability. Stone tools can be dated from the rock layers (strata) in which they are found.

Classification — From Five Kingdoms to Three Domains

Traditionally, living organisms were classified into five kingdoms: Animals, Plants, Fungi, Protists and Prokaryotes. This system was based on observable features such as cell structure and how organisms obtained food.

More recently, genetic analysis has shown that the five-kingdom system does not accurately reflect evolutionary relationships. Scientists now use the three-domain system instead:

Archaea — primitive prokaryotes, often found in extreme environments. Bacteria — true bacteria (prokaryotes). Eukarya — all organisms with eukaryotic cells (animals, plants, fungi and protists). Genetic analysis revealed that Archaea are more different from Bacteria than was previously thought, which is why they were separated into their own domain.

The five-kingdom system relied on physical features, which can be misleading — organisms may look similar but be distantly related (convergent evolution). Genetic analysis compares DNA sequences directly, giving a more accurate picture of evolutionary relationships. This led Carl Woese to propose the three-domain system in 1990.

lessons.title: Genetic Engineering
lessons.description: How genetic engineering works, its stages, and the benefits and risks of GM organisms.
lessons.content_html:
Selective Breeding

Selective breeding (also called artificial selection) is the process by which humans choose organisms with desirable characteristics and breed them together. This is repeated over many generations until the desired trait is strongly expressed in the population.

Selective breeding has been used for thousands of years. Examples include breeding food plants for higher yield, disease resistance or improved taste, and breeding domesticated animals for traits such as increased milk production in cows, faster growth in chickens or tameness in dogs.

The process works because the parents with the best characteristics are selected, so their alleles are more likely to be passed on. Over many generations, the frequency of the desirable alleles increases in the population.

Key Fact

Selective breeding: choose parents with desirable traits → breed them → select the best offspring → repeat over many generations. Used to improve food plants and domesticated animals.

A major risk of selective breeding is inbreeding. Because only organisms with similar desirable traits are bred, the gene pool narrows. This reduces genetic variation, making the population more vulnerable to new diseases or environmental changes. In animals, inbreeding can also lead to health problems — for example, breathing difficulties in flat-faced dog breeds.

What Is Genetic Engineering?

Genetic engineering is the process of modifying the genome of an organism to introduce desirable characteristics. Unlike selective breeding, which works within a species, genetic engineering can transfer genes between completely different species. An organism that contains a gene from a different species is called a genetically modified organism (GMO) or transgenic organism.

The Main Stages of Genetic Engineering

The Edexcel specification requires you to describe the main stages of genetic engineering, including the use of restriction enzymes, ligase, sticky ends and vectors.

Step 1 — Identify and cut out the desired gene. Restriction enzymes are used to cut the desired gene out of the DNA of the donor organism. These enzymes cut at specific base sequences, leaving short unpaired stretches of bases called sticky ends.

Step 2 — Open the vector. The same restriction enzyme is used to cut open a vector — a carrier molecule that will transport the gene into the host organism. Common vectors include bacterial plasmids and viruses. Because the same restriction enzyme is used, the vector has complementary sticky ends.

Step 3 — Insert the gene. The desired gene is inserted into the vector. The complementary sticky ends of the gene and the vector pair up. Ligase enzyme is then used to seal the gene into the vector by joining the sugar-phosphate backbone, creating recombinant DNA.

Step 4 — Transfer to host organism. The vector carries the gene into the host organism’s cells. If the gene is successfully taken up, the host organism will produce the protein coded for by the inserted gene, giving it the desired characteristic.

Key Fact

Genetic engineering: restriction enzymes cut out the gene (leaving sticky ends) → same enzyme opens the vector → gene inserted, sticky ends pair up → ligase seals the join → vector transfers gene to host organism.

Examples of Genetic Engineering

In agriculture, crops such as soya and maize have been genetically modified to be resistant to herbicides or to produce their own insecticide (Bt crops). Golden rice has been engineered to produce beta-carotene (vitamin A) to help prevent deficiency in developing countries.

In medicine, the gene for human insulin has been inserted into bacteria. These bacteria are grown in fermenters and produce large quantities of human insulin to treat diabetes. This replaced insulin extracted from pig or cow pancreases, which sometimes caused allergic reactions.

Benefits and Risks of Genetic Engineering and Selective Breeding

The Edexcel specification requires you to evaluate the benefits and risks of both genetic engineering and selective breeding in modern agriculture and medicine, including practical and ethical implications.

Benefits of genetic engineering: genes can be transferred between species that could never breed naturally; crops can be made pest-resistant, reducing pesticide use; medicines like insulin can be produced cheaply and reliably; Golden Rice could reduce vitamin A deficiency in developing countries.

Risks and concerns: GM crops could cross-pollinate with wild plants, spreading modified genes into the environment in unpredictable ways; there are concerns about the long-term effects of eating GM food (though no evidence of harm has been found); some people have ethical objections to ‘playing God’ with organisms’ DNA; GM seeds are often patented, making farmers dependent on seed companies.

Selective breeding is considered more ‘natural’ but reduces genetic diversity, which can cause health problems and makes populations vulnerable to disease. Genetic engineering is faster and more precise, but raises more ethical and environmental concerns.

lessons.title: Health, Disease and Medicines
lessons.description: Communicable and non-communicable diseases, the immune system and drug development.
lessons.content_html:
Defining Health

The World Health Organization (WHO) defines health as a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being — not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. This means that being healthy involves more than just not being ill; it includes emotional wellbeing and having good social relationships.

Diseases fall into two broad categories. Communicable diseases can be spread from one organism to another and are caused by pathogens. Non-communicable diseases cannot be passed on and are often linked to lifestyle or genetic factors. The presence of one disease can increase susceptibility to others — for example, a weakened immune system from HIV can make a person more vulnerable to tuberculosis.

Pathogens and Common Infections

A pathogen is a disease-causing organism. There are four types of pathogen: bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists. The Edexcel specification requires you to know several named infections:

Cholera (caused by bacteria) — causes severe diarrhoea and dehydration. Spread through contaminated water. Prevented by clean water supplies and sanitation.

Tuberculosis (TB, caused by bacteria) — causes lung damage, persistent cough and weight loss. Spread by airborne droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Prevented by vaccination (BCG) and treating infected people with antibiotics.

Chalara ash dieback (caused by a fungus) — causes leaf loss and bark lesions in ash trees. Spread by airborne spores carried by wind. Difficult to prevent; infected trees are often removed to slow the spread.

Malaria (caused by a protist) — damages blood cells and the liver, causing fever and chills. Spread by animal vectors (female Anopheles mosquitoes). Prevented by mosquito nets, insecticides and draining stagnant water where mosquitoes breed.

HIV (a virus) — destroys white blood cells, weakening the immune system. If untreated, it leads to AIDS. HIV is a sexually transmitted infection (STI) and can also be spread through blood-to-blood contact (e.g. shared needles). Prevented by using condoms and screening blood donations.

Chlamydia (caused by bacteria) — the most common STI in the UK. Often has no symptoms but can cause infertility if untreated. Spread by unprotected sexual contact. Prevented by using condoms and treated with antibiotics. Screening programmes help identify and treat cases early.

Key Fact

Learn the six named infections: cholera (bacteria, water), TB (bacteria, airborne), Chalara (fungus, airborne), malaria (protist, mosquito vector), HIV (virus, sexual/blood), chlamydia (bacteria, sexual).

The Body’s Defences

The human body has physical barriers to prevent pathogens from entering: the skin provides a continuous barrier; mucus in the respiratory tract traps pathogens; and cilia (tiny hair-like structures) sweep mucus and trapped pathogens towards the throat to be swallowed.

The body also has chemical defences: lysozymes in tears, saliva and nasal secretions destroy bacteria by breaking down their cell walls. Hydrochloric acid in the stomach (pH 1–2) kills most pathogens that are swallowed with food or drink.

The Immune System

If pathogens get past the body’s physical and chemical defences, the immune system responds. Pathogens have unique molecules on their surface called antigens. White blood cells called lymphocytes detect these antigens and produce specific antibodies that bind to the antigens and mark the pathogen for destruction.

After the infection is cleared, memory lymphocytes remain in the blood. If the same pathogen enters the body again, memory lymphocytes trigger a secondary response — a much faster and stronger production of antibodies, destroying the pathogen before symptoms develop.

Key Fact

Immune response: pathogen enters → antigens trigger lymphocytes → antibodies produced → pathogen destroyed → memory lymphocytes remain for faster secondary response.

Vaccination

Vaccination (immunisation) involves injecting a dead or inactive form of a pathogen into the body. The antigens on the inactive pathogen still trigger an immune response — lymphocytes produce antibodies and memory lymphocytes are formed. The person does not become ill because the pathogen is inactive. If the real pathogen enters the body later, memory lymphocytes enable a rapid secondary response, preventing the disease.

Antibiotics and Drug Development

Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or prevent them from reproducing. They work by inhibiting specific cell processes in the bacterium — for example, preventing cell wall formation. Antibiotics cannot treat viral infections because viruses reproduce inside host cells and do not have their own cell machinery.

Developing new medicines involves many stages: discovery (identifying a potential new drug from plants, microorganisms or computer modelling), development (refining the compound), preclinical testing (testing on cells, tissues and animals to check for toxicity and effectiveness) and clinical testing (trials on healthy volunteers and then patients, including double-blind trials with placebos to ensure the drug is both safe and effective).

Non-Communicable Diseases and Lifestyle

Many non-communicable diseases are caused by the interaction of several factors, including genetics, lifestyle and environment. Examples include cardiovascular diseases, many cancers, and some lung and liver diseases.

Lifestyle factors that increase the risk of non-communicable diseases include: poor diet and lack of exercise leading to obesity (measured using BMI = mass in kg ÷ height in m², and waist-to-hip ratio); excessive alcohol consumption leading to liver disease and cirrhosis; and smoking which damages blood vessels and increases the risk of coronary heart disease, stroke and lung cancer.

Treatments for cardiovascular disease include lifestyle changes (improved diet, more exercise, stopping smoking), life-long medication (statins to lower cholesterol, blood-thinning drugs) and surgical procedures (stents to open blocked arteries, bypass surgery). Each treatment has advantages and disadvantages — for example, medication must be taken daily and may have side effects, while surgery carries risks but can be immediately effective.
